extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, and law students handling U.S. patent re-issue applications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive standards governing U.S. applications for re-issue of patents: required contents, oath and statement, limits on amended specifications/drawings/models, examination on merits (novelty, utility, abandonment), identity with original, interferences, appeals, and effect of a re-issue on term and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis and contents of re-issue application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a re-issue must be based upon a single original patent and must show the original to have been defective through mistake; it comprises a petition, an oath, an abstract of title, and the amended specification, accompanied by such drawings and model as the nature of the case may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition prays for leave to surrender the original patent and for a re-issue upon the amended specification. Petition should be signed by the true owners unless special assignment-date rules apply (e.g., if patent was granted/transferred since July 8, 1870, inventor's signature and present owners' written assent may be required). If the original patent is lost, deliver a certified copy and an affidavit of loss. (Cited cases: Selden v. Stockwell; National Spring Co. v. Union Car Spring Mfg. Co.; Ex parte Fassett.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract of title and ownership disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract of title must disclose the names of all persons owning any undivided interest in the original patent and must disclose the original patent (or a certified copy and affidavit of its loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract must accompany the application for re-issue. If the inventor has deceased and the petition bears assignee signatures, the fact of death must be duly stated. (Cited: Ex parte Fassett; cases cited in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath requirements and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the petition must be signed by the inventor, the oath must also be made by him; otherwise it should be made by the applicants. The oath must state particularly that the applicant believes the original patent to be inoperative or invalid, with reasons, specifying defects or insufficiencies in the description or excessive matter in the claims, pointing out the errors constituting inadvertence/accident/mistake, and alleging such errors occurred without fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath must also disclose foreign patents for the same invention (if any) and the extent to which the invention has been used in the U.S., similar to original applications. Under certain statutory dates/rules (e.g., acts of 1870/1871), different persons' oaths may suffice. The requirement for a detailed statement under oath is imperative; omission or insufficient statements can prevent examination or render re-issue void. (Cited: National Spring Co. v. Union Car Spring Mfg. Co.; Ex parte Whitely; Poage v. McGowan.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and factual nature of the supporting statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement filed with a re-issue application must set out the facts on which the application is based, not merely the opinions or conclusions of the preparer; the statement must be sufficient before the re-issue will be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere allegation such as 'misunderstanding' is insufficient. The rule requiring a detailed factual statement is not retroactive. If the statement is insufficient, the examiner will not examine the re-issue on the merits and the proceedings will terminate; if sufficient, the merits are then examined. (Cited: Ex parte Timken; Ex parte Wilkins; Ex parte Underwood.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on amended specification and prohibition on new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of the amended specification must correspond with that of the original unless some sufficient reason for a change appears; the identity of the invention must be preserved and no unnecessary divergence from the original wording should be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New names, new uses, or new descriptive matter tend to create uncertainty and may be stricken; except to correct errors where additional or substituted phraseology is required, the Patent Office restricts the amended specification to statements made in the original. Re-issue specifications are treated more strictly than originals to avoid allowing patentees to appropriate later developments by frequent re-issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for drawings and models in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: New drawings must accompany the specification when the invention is susceptible of delineation and must conform in style, number and artistic perfection to regulations governing original drawings; new drawings may vary from the old only where the variation appears in the original model or relates to unimportant matter not affecting the invention claimed. Amendment of the model is limited to features found in the original drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great care should be exercised to exclude new matter if the original patent lacked drawings or model. Extraneous evidence about a model destroyed by fire or loss will generally not be received on a re-issue application. (Cited: Ex parte Gottstein; McWilliams.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing, fees, pendency, and interim rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The application, with statutory fees, is presented to the Patent Office and entitles the applicant to consideration. Filing does not preclude the applicant from resuming rights under the former patent; at any time before the re-issue is granted the applicant may withdraw the application, revoke the surrender, and be restored to his original position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Commissioner refuses to proceed, mandamus may lie to compel action. Hearings on re-issue applications take precedence and may be expedited when the original patent is near expiry. Even if fees are not yet accepted, once the applicant has done all he can to make the application effective, the Commissioner has duty to hear it. (Cited: Commissioner v. Whitely; Ex parte Evarts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination on merits — applicable standards and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification annexed to a re-issue application is subject to the same formal corrections as an original. Examination on the merits inquires into patentability of the invention, identity with the invention attempted to be covered by the former patent, and the cause of the alleged error in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability (novelty, utility, abandonment, priority) is judged as on original applications and the relevant state of the art is that at the date of the original application. Repetition of exact original claims does not exempt them from examination. Abandonment may be shown by more than two years' public use/sale before the original application, omission to claim after clear description and unreasonable delay, or other conduct indicating dedication to the public. (Cited: Carroll v. Morse; Funck v. Doty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity test between re-issue claims and original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue invention is not identical to the original unless all essential characteristics of the invention claimed in the re-issue were described or attempted to be described in the original specification, drawings, or model as part of the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In machine patents identity must appear by comparison of drawings and models (which can be amended only by each other). Where no drawings/models exist, extrinsic proof may be offered to establish identity. Examiners must be guided by statutes and judicial decisions, not personal discretion. Parol evidence is not admissible to enlarge the scope beyond the original disclosure. (Cited: Giant Powder Co. v. California Powder Works; Shaw v. Colwell Lead Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of cause of defects and absence of fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The affidavit of the applicant is prima facie proof that the error in the original occurred through inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intention, but this may be contradicted by Patent Office records, officers' affidavits, or other satisfactory evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner may examine proofs to ascertain identity and cause, but must protect applicant secrecy. The existence of inadvertence/mistake (and lack of fraud) must be established before legally allowing re-issue. Subsequent conduct of the inventor is relevant only as it sheds light on his original intention; later acts generally do not estop him from amending unless they show intent at the time of original application. (Cited: Ex parte Conklin; Basparly Conklin; Newton v. Furst & Bradley Mfg.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference rules affecting re-issue applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue application can be placed in interference with a pending original application, another re-issue application, or an unexpired patent whenever the inventions claimed are apparently identical; an interference will be declared under specified rules and conditions (e.g., when original applications were pending at same time or when an oath of prior inventive act is made).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interference is declared between a patent and an application and, during the interference, a re-issue is applied for, the re-issue application is examined on its individual merits and, if allowed, substitutes for the original patent in the interference. Re-issue applications that initially do not claim the interfered invention may be amended to insert such claims and be admitted. Proceedings in interference follow the same rules whether applications are original or re-issue. (Cited: Ex parte Zay; statutory rules summarized.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of examination and effect of insufficient statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must first determine the sufficiency of the statement accompanying a re-issue application; if the statement is insufficient the re-issue will not be examined on the merits, and the proceedings will terminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of a re-issue application will not be examined on their merits in connection with the sufficiency question but in proper order once the statement is sufficient. An insufficient affidavit or conclusory statement (e.g., 'not fully valid and available') may render the re-issue void. (Cited: Ex parte Timken; Poage v. McGowan.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and finality of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: From adverse decisions of examiners on questions relating to merits, an appeal lies to the examiners-in-chief, the Commissioner, the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia, and to the U.S. Supreme Court, except in interference cases where the Commissioner's decision is final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after allowance by examiners, the Commissioner retains control and may withhold a patent on sufficient grounds. If one Commissioner refused a re-issue, a successor should not grant it without careful re-examination and clear conviction that the prior judgment was erroneous. (Cited: Ex parte Hunt; Ex parte Hant.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Date, term, and legal effect of a re-issued patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent bears the date of the original for all purposes except as the foundation of an action for infringement; when term is expressed in years the term runs from the grant of the original; all rights of parties claiming under the re-issue are held to have accrued when the original patent issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender of the original patent extinguishes actions under it and abates suits pending at the date of re-issue; a re-issue only affects suits subsequently begun. When the original was limited by duration of a foreign patent, the re-issue is subject to same limitation. (Cited: Whitely v. Fisher; Jones v. Barker; United States Stamping Co. v. King.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot impair third-party or non-consenting owners' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: No re-issue of a patent can affect the rights of non-consenting owners or other third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law holds that re-issues do not bind non-consenting owners or third parties; re-issue is an action between patentee and public/patent office but cannot operate to enlarge rights as against third parties who did not consent. (Cited: Potter v. Braundsdorf; Potter v. Holland.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using re-issues to appropriate subsequent improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules and practice limit a patentee from using re-issues to interpolate new uses, new descriptive matter, or new names so as to keep pace with advancements in the art and appropriate improvements made by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While original applications are given liberal latitude in language choice, re-issue applications are subjected to strict construction; the applicant must show good reason for new terms or descriptive matter, or such matter will be stricken out to prevent fraud and unwarrantable departure from the original invention. (Cited: Hatch v. Moffitt; Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. v. Haish.)
